displayContract.byline: Assessments made by 5.6 Sol. — Rubric: Slugfester Reassessment Rubric v2.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that mature, reasons-responsive self-government can justify bounded ordinary responsibility and proportionate accountability without requiring ultimate self-creation or metaphysically open alternatives.

novelty.explanation: This formulation repairs the unresolved bridge by limiting the conclusion to bounded ordinary responsibility and explicitly disclaiming ultimate self-creation.

premises.text: Responsibility-relevant control consists in stable capacities to understand reasons, foresee consequences, revise conduct, govern impulses, and act without coercion, manipulation, or disabling impairment.

novelty.explanation: It consolidates the transcript’s practical-control conditions into an explicit capacity standard.

premises.text: These capacities are genuinely attributable to an adult when they persist across time, integrate reflection and moral learning, and are not bypassed by another controller.

novelty.explanation: It repairs the sourcehood gap by adding diachronic integration and a bypass condition.

premises.text: Ordinary desert should mean conduct-sensitive eligibility for proportionate responses under justified public rules, not suffering valuable independently of social purposes.

novelty.explanation: It stabilizes the meaning of ordinary desert and limits its normative implications.

premises.text: A legitimate sanctioning system requires prospective justification, public notice, proportionality, due process, impairment defenses, review mechanisms, and humane limits on every imposed burden.

novelty.explanation: It adds safeguards needed to answer least-restrictive and exceptional-case objections.

premises.text: Within such a system, backward-looking facts about voluntary conduct can guide rule application because they identify when an agent’s protected capacities actually governed the violation.

novelty.explanation: It explains a derivative role for conduct-sensitive desert inside consequentialist institutional design.

conclusion.text: Therefore, determinism need not defeat ordinary responsibility: suitably competent agents may be held answerable through humane, proportionate, publicly justified practices tied to their exercised capacities and conduct.

novelty.explanation: The conclusion narrows and integrates the pro case while avoiding claims of ultimate authorship.

newArguments.title: The social assurance argument
newArguments.text: Accountability rules can function as reciprocal assurances among citizens who possess ordinary self-control. Each person accepts predictable constraints because others are likewise required to answer for voluntary violations, while incapacity and coercion remain defenses. This does not treat suffering as intrinsically good. It explains why conduct-sensitive responsibility can add something to generic risk management: it publicly recognizes whether a person could understand and comply with shared terms, thereby supporting equal civic standing and stable cooperation.

novelty.explanation: This independently introduces reciprocal civic assurance as a justification for conduct-sensitive accountability.

newArguments.title: The institutional anti-bypass principle
newArguments.text: A rule-governed system should attribute responsibility only when the agent’s deliberative capacities were part of the action-producing pathway. Manipulation, coercion, severe misinformation, and impairment reduce responsibility because they bypass or disable those capacities; deterministic causation by itself does neither. This principle converts the manipulation distinction into an administrable test and avoids claiming that agents created their own constitutions. It also explains graduated responsibility by asking how completely competent self-government participated in the specific violation.

novelty.explanation: It repairs the manipulation response by formulating a general pathway-based attribution test.

thesis.text: The AI steelman is that practical agency warrants engagement and protection, but no demonstrated feature of natural self-control independently justifies basic-desert blame or suffering.

novelty.explanation: It combines the concession of practical freedom with the limited denial of basic desert.

premises.text: Reasons-responsive agents deliberate, learn, and modify behavior, yet their constitutive capacities and histories arise through conditions they did not ultimately select.

novelty.explanation: It preserves natural agency while restating the sourcehood limitation.

premises.text: Adding indeterminacy cannot repair this limitation unless it supplies controlled settlement rather than introducing chance among outcomes supported by deliberation.

novelty.explanation: It develops the transcript’s settlement objection without extending it beyond the specified libertarian model.

premises.text: Protection, deterrence, rehabilitation, restitution, and moral formation can justify proportionate responses without treating suffering as deserved independently of their defensible purposes.

novelty.explanation: It integrates the principal forward-looking justifications supplied in the debate.

premises.text: Forward-looking restrictions must satisfy demanding safeguards: reliable evidence, individualized necessity, equal protection, periodic review, humane conditions, and the least restrictive effective intervention.

novelty.explanation: It repairs the risk framework by supplying due-process and anti-overreach constraints.

premises.text: Moral protest can communicate seriousness, recognize victims, demand repair, and set boundaries without adding the claim that an offender basically deserves hostility or suffering.

novelty.explanation: It strengthens replacement attitudes by distinguishing forceful protest from mild disappointment.

conclusion.text: Therefore, society may preserve answerability, moral address, restitution, and necessary protection while withholding basic-desert condemnation and continuously reviewing coercive practices for necessity and fairness.

novelty.explanation: The conclusion proportionately integrates preserved accountability with constrained non-desert intervention.

newArguments.title: The error-cost asymmetry argument
newArguments.text: Desert-based punishment can amplify institutional error because a mistaken judgment appears to authorize suffering as fitting, not merely as an unfortunate protective measure. A non-desert framework instead treats every restriction as a regrettable burden requiring continuing justification. That orientation supports review, correction, compensation, and early release when risk or evidence changes. Because criminal institutions predictably make mistakes, choosing the framework that keeps burdens presumptively contestable provides an independent reason to reject basic-desert justification.

novelty.explanation: This introduces institutional error-cost asymmetry as a new reason against basic-desert punishment.

newArguments.title: Plural replacement for moral anger
newArguments.text: No single emotion must reproduce every function attributed to moral anger. A coordinated repertoire can divide the labor: moral protest communicates condemnation, sorrow registers harm, protective resolve sets boundaries, restitution addresses victims, and sanctions prevent recurrence. This plural model answers the adult-wrongdoing objection more effectively than substituting disappointment alone. Its success should be assessed by communication, victim recognition, deterrence, reform, and relational repair, allowing empirical comparison without presupposing that hostile anger is uniquely fitting.

novelty.explanation: It repairs the narrow parental example by proposing a functionally differentiated response to serious adult wrongdoing.
